claims.claim: Authoritarian regimes authorize institutions and processes that concentrate power in the hands of a single leader or a small group, and those rulers need not seek or secure the approval of the people to govern.
Authoritarian rule is characterized by three recurring features: concentrated power, limited participation, and controlled information.
Authoritarian regimes seek legitimacy through control of education, restrictions on criticism, and propaganda, while also relying on physical force backed by large militaries and police.

Authoritarian regimes can be classified into types, including personal dictatorship, one-party rule, and military rule; real regimes often blend these forms, and some classifications add hereditary monarchy and theocracy.
Authoritarian rule persists through a combination of coercion, co-optation (buying loyalty with privileges), and, in some cases, genuine popular support.

Authoritarian regimes fall along a spectrum from hard authoritarianism, which relies heavily on physical force and pervasive suppression, to soft authoritarianism, which tolerates some economic freedom and limited public debate while keeping genuine political power out of reach.

The decisive difference between democracy and authoritarianism is accountability: democratic rulers can be removed by citizens through free and fair elections and are checked by courts, legislatures, and a free press, whereas authoritarian rulers face no such brake.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Classifications of regime types vary across textbooks: some add hereditary monarchy and theocracy as distinct forms of authoritarian rule, while others fold them into personal rule or treat them as separate categories.
positions: OpenStax's Introduction to Political Science presents dictatorship, one-party rule, and military rule as the main types of authoritarian regime.
Some comparative-politics references (e.g., Britannica) note additional forms such as hereditary monarchy and theocracy.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the three most widely used types as the standard core and explicitly acknowledges that some classifications add further forms. No live country examples are used, so classification disputes over particular cases do not arise.
